MSK–SKIN · WEEK 17 · LECTURE COMPANION

Skeletal Muscle Physiology

Ruchi Patel, PhD · Medical College of Georgia
From α-motor neuron excitation to calcium signaling, force production, fatigue and training adaptation.

01 · Calcium and contraction02 · Force generation03 · Fatigue04 · Conditioning

Learning Objectives

  1. Describe the role of calcium in excitation–contraction coupling in skeletal muscle contraction.
  2. Discuss factors influencing summation of muscle force and ways to increase contraction strength.
  3. Explain fatigue through energy depletion, metabolite accumulation, neural drive, and calcium handling.
  4. Explain adaptations to conditioning: hypertrophy, oxidative capacity, and fiber-type composition.
Big picture. An α-motor neuron initiates an action potential → the T-tubule voltage sensor opens the SR calcium-release channel → calcium exposes actin binding sites → ATP-powered myosin cycling produces force. Force also depends on sarcomere length, load, recruited motor units, and stimulation frequency. Fatigue disrupts the chain; training remodels it.

Primary source: Dr. Ruchi Patel, Skeletal Muscle Physiology, 27-slide MCG lecture. Connections from First Aid 2025 are explicitly marked. Lecture-specific terminology is maintained, including the slide’s Type IIB nomenclature.

1Calcium and excitation–contraction coupling

Muscle is approximately 40% of body mass; besides movement it provides support and produces heat. The core energy conversion is chemical energy (ATP) → mechanical work through interaction of myosin with actin.

Activation requires an α-motor neuron

In this lecture, skeletal muscle contraction is initiated by somatic α-motor neurons, not by autonomic or intrinsic pacemaker activity. A motor unit is one motor neuron and every muscle fiber it innervates. A single neuron branches to many fibers; each individual fiber normally receives control from one α-motor neuron. An action potential in that neuron stimulates every fiber belonging to its motor unit.

The electrical signal becomes a calcium signal

  1. Presynaptic motor-neuron action potential causes acetylcholine (ACh) release at the neuromuscular junction.
  2. ACh binds the nicotinic ACh receptor (a ligand-gated cation channel), producing the end-plate potential.
  3. Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels generate a muscle action potential that propagates along sarcolemma and down T-tubules.
  4. The T-tubule dihydropyridine (DHP) receptor senses depolarization and mechanically activates the ryanodine receptor (RyR) on sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR).
  5. SR Ca²⁺ enters cytosol and binds troponin, displacing tropomyosin from actin’s myosin-binding sites.
  6. Myosin cross bridges cycle, generating tension; SERCA (SR Ca²⁺-ATPase) returns Ca²⁺ to SR for relaxation.
MUST KNOW
Key skeletal-versus-cardiac distinction: the DHP receptor serves as a voltage sensor mechanically coupled to RyR. As emphasized on slide 9, skeletal muscle does not require extracellular Ca²⁺ entry through DHP to trigger contraction; the contracting Ca²⁺ is released from the SR.

What Ca²⁺ actually changes

At low cytosolic calcium, tropomyosin physically prevents productive myosin attachment. With Ca²⁺ bound to troponin, the binding site becomes accessible. Calcium permits cycling; ATP powers cycling and detachment. Removing calcium stops new cycling rather than directly shortening the muscle.

Cross-bridge cycle and ATP

  1. ATP-bound myosin is detached in a low-energy conformation.
  2. Myosin ATPase hydrolyzes ATP to ADP + Pi, cocking the head into high-energy position.
  3. If calcium has exposed actin, the energized head binds actin.
  4. Pi and ADP release accompany the power stroke, pulling actin toward the M line.
  5. A new ATP binds myosin to detach it; without ATP, detachment cannot occur.
EXAM TRAP
ATP binding detaches myosin; ATP hydrolysis re-cocks it. Calcium binding to troponin exposes the site but does not substitute for ATP.

Sliding filament and band changes

A sarcomere spans Z disk to Z disk. The A band corresponds to thick filament length, I band contains only thin filament, and H zone contains only thick filament. During contraction: Z disks converge, I band and H zone shrink, A band remains constant. Filaments slide rather than becoming shorter.

ATP supply and single twitches

The lecture lists three major sources: phosphocreatine (~5–8 sec), glycogen glycolysis (~1 min), and oxidative phosphorylation for prolonged activity (with fat increasingly important for the longest durations). ATP also fuels SERCA reuptake and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump. A twitch has latent (EC coupling), contraction, and relaxation phases. Force develops more slowly than the action potential and persists after it.

FIRST AID CONNECTION
Malignant hyperthermia: in susceptible patients, certain anesthetic triggers cause excessive SR Ca²⁺ release via RyR1-related dysregulation. Sustained contraction and ATP consumption explain hypermetabolism; dantrolene inhibits RyR-mediated calcium release. This is a board association with the lecture’s DHP–RyR–SR mechanism, not a lecture claim.
Why can muscle relaxation require ATP even after neural stimulation stops?
SERCA uses ATP to pump cytosolic Ca²⁺ into SR, allowing tropomyosin to block actin sites again. ATP is also needed for cross-bridge detachment.
What happens to A band, I band, and H zone during shortening?
A band remains the same; I band and H zone become narrower as overlap increases.

2Force summation and strength

Muscle force depends on more than whether an action potential occurs. The lecture separates intrinsic mechanics (length–tension and force–velocity) from neural control (motor-unit recruitment and stimulation frequency), with fiber phenotype also altering force and endurance.

Length–tension: why resting length matters

Active tension depends on how many useful actin–myosin cross bridges can form. Very short sarcomeres have excessive overlap/interference, intermediate lengths permit maximal effective overlap, and lengths with no overlap cannot generate active force. Passive tension rises as elastic elements such as titin are stretched; total tension includes active and passive contributions.

COMMON CONFUSION
Passive tension is stretch of elastic components (no cross-bridge cycling required), whereas active tension is ATP-dependent force generated by cross bridges. Greater length does not always mean greater active force.

Force–velocity: load slows shortening

As an opposing afterload increases, the shortening velocity falls. Conversely, a muscle shortens fastest at minimal load, when force is low. Power = Force × Velocity; maximal power occurs at an intermediate combination rather than at maximal force or maximal shortening velocity. The lecture’s graph places it around one-third of maximum velocity.

Fiber phenotype determines performance

CharacteristicSlow Type I (red)Fast Type IIB (white; lecture terminology)
Myosin ATPase / speedSlower cycling, low shortening velocityFast cycling, high shortening velocity
Diameter / forceSmaller; lower forceLarger; greater force
Metabolic profileHigh capillary density, myoglobin, mitochondria; oxidativeMore glycolytic enzymes; fewer mitochondria, lower capillary density
PerformancePosture and prolonged activity; fatigue resistantRapid powerful bursts; fatigues readily
BOARD / CLINICAL ENRICHMENT
Human skeletal-muscle teaching commonly subdivides fast fibers into IIa and IIx; the lecture uses Type IIB for its fast/white comparison. Preserve the lecturer’s wording for in-house assessment rather than silently substituting nomenclature.

Recruitment = more units; summation = faster firing within units

In motor-unit recruitment, increasing the number of activated α-motor neurons engages more muscle fibers. By the size principle, low-threshold, small, fatigue-resistant units are recruited first; larger high-threshold units support stronger bursts. In frequency summation, repeated action potentials arrive before complete twitch relaxation; successive Ca²⁺ transients generate superimposed force. At high enough frequency, fused tetanus produces smooth sustained tension.

HIGH YIELD
Recruitment increases the number of muscle fibers contracting. Frequency summation increases force in fibers already active. Neither is the same as increasing the amplitude of an individual muscle action potential.
A muscle is stimulated twice before its first twitch fully relaxes. Why is the second force larger?
Residual cross-bridge activity and renewed cytosolic Ca²⁺ allow the next twitch to add to the first rather than starting at baseline.
What does a high afterload do to shortening velocity, and where is power highest?
Greater afterload reduces velocity. Power peaks at an intermediate force–velocity combination, not at either maximum.

3Mechanisms of muscle fatigue

Muscle fatigue means a decline in maximal force or task performance during activity. The lecture distinguishes perceptual or mental contributions from physical performance and identifies both central and peripheral mechanisms; do not assume every episode of weakness reflects ATP depletion alone.

Where in the pathway does performance fail?

LevelLecture mechanismFunctional consequence
Central neural driveAltered central neurotransmitters, reduced motor cortex drive, declining motor neuron firing, changed sensory inputFewer/weaker activation commands reach motor units
Membrane excitationExtracellular K⁺ accumulationAction-potential propagation/excitability may be impaired
Calcium handlingElevated free Mg²⁺ or inorganic phosphate (Pi) impair SR Ca²⁺ releaseLess Ca²⁺ binds troponin, so fewer sites support cross bridges
Fuel and oxygenDecreased blood flow and oxygen, muscle glycogen depletionLess sustained ATP production to support cycling and ion pumps
Metabolite accumulationH⁺, lactate, Pi, reactive oxygen species (ROS)Reduced pH and oxidation may impair SR release, troponin sensitivity, pumps and contractile proteins

Why metabolites affect force

When metabolites accumulate, the effect is not merely an abstract “acid buildup.” The lecture proposes changes in Ca²⁺ release from SR, troponin C sensitivity to Ca²⁺, and the cross-bridge cycle. Increased Pi also suppresses SR release, and ROS can oxidatively modify Na⁺/K⁺ pumps, myofilaments, DHP receptors, and RyR. Each produces a specific failure point in the activation-to-force sequence.

EXAM TRAP
Central fatigue = reduced neural drive to muscles; peripheral fatigue = reduced force capacity of activated muscle. The two are mechanistically distinct and may occur together.
FOUNDATIONS LINK
Ion gradients sustain electrical excitability; calcium gradients permit excitation–contraction coupling; oxidative phosphorylation replenishes ATP. Fatigue illustrates how membrane physiology, metabolism, and signaling converge on a single mechanical output.
How can increased extracellular K⁺ reduce force even if actin and myosin are intact?
It may disturb membrane excitability and action potential propagation, reducing successful excitation–contraction coupling.
Why could high intracellular Pi impair force through more than one mechanism?
Pi may reduce SR calcium release, and altered metabolic conditions can directly impair effective contractile function.

4Exercise adaptation and remodeling

Training changes skeletal muscle phenotype. Which adaptation dominates depends on load, duration, frequency, intensity, age, and genetics. Distinguish gaining capacity to produce force from improving the ability to sustain force.

Endurance versus strength training

AdaptationEndurance / aerobic trainingStrength / power training
Typical stimulusLower load, longer durationHigher load, shorter duration
Principal cellular shiftMore mitochondria and oxidative enzymes; better mitochondrial functionMore actin/myosin synthesis and myofibrils; increased cross-sectional area
CirculationIncreased capillary density and O₂ deliveryNot the principal change emphasized here
Neural responseImproved sustained workRecruitment pattern changes and increased firing rates
Fiber proportionsPossible shift toward slow oxidative phenotypePossible shift toward fast glycolytic phenotype

Remodeling: growth takes different forms

Hypertrophy is larger existing fibers: synthesis of actin/myosin, addition of myofibrillar material, and increased fiber cross-sectional area. It is common after resistance training and can become apparent within weeks. Hyperplasia means additional fiber number and is rare in human skeletal muscle. Lengthening occurs during normal growth and adds shortening capacity/velocity without the same change in maximum force emphasized for hypertrophy.

Atrophy: what changes and why?

Atrophy reduces muscle mass and strength. Lecture examples include disuse (sedentary behavior, casting, weightlessness), neurogenic causes (denervation, motor-neuron disease, peripheral neuropathy), and disease/age causes (sarcopenia, malnutrition, cachexia). Prolonged disuse can lead to actual fiber loss, which is especially difficult to reverse.

CLINICAL CONNECTION
Immobilization after an injury can reduce muscle size and force despite intact neural pathways. By contrast, denervation removes normal motor input and can produce neurogenic atrophy; identical outward weakness need not indicate identical biology.
MSK CONNECTION
Link this lecture to the prior muscle histology lecture: a change in myofibrillar content alters fiber cross-sectional area, while muscle-stem-cell and fibro-adipogenic progenitor biology may influence the quality of regeneration versus replacement by fat/fibrosis.
Which adaptations best explain an endurance athlete’s increased fatigue resistance?
More mitochondria/oxidative enzymes and capillary density support sustained ATP synthesis and oxygen delivery.
Does a larger muscle fiber necessarily mean more muscle fibers?
No. Hypertrophy enlarges existing fibers; hyperplasia adds fibers and is rare.

MASTER THESE BEFORE MOVING ON

  1. DHP–RyR–SR coupling: know why cytosolic calcium rises without needing extracellular calcium influx through DHP in skeletal muscle. This distinguishes skeletal from cardiac coupling.
  2. Calcium versus ATP: Ca²⁺ exposes actin sites; ATP powers myosin cycling, detachment, and calcium reuptake. This predicts failure modes.
  3. Length–tension versus force–velocity: one describes overlap-dependent force; the other the tradeoff between load and shortening speed.
  4. Recruitment versus summation: recruit more fibers versus stimulate existing fibers more frequently. Both change whole-muscle tension.
  5. Fatigue versus remodeling: fatigue is a short-term reduction in performance; training and atrophy change the tissue’s lasting capacity.

THE MOST USEFUL FIRST AID CONNECTIONS

1. Malignant hyperthermia: uncontrolled SR calcium release and hypermetabolism from dysregulated RyR signaling; dantrolene limits calcium release. 2. Glycogen-storage disorders (e.g., McArdle): failure of muscle glycogen utilization may cause exercise intolerance, illuminating the ATP-fuel hierarchy. These are focused First Aid connections, not additions to Dr. Patel’s stated learning objectives.

Source: Dr. Patel, Skeletal Muscle Physiology, slides 1–27. Supplemental board associations: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (2025), relevant malignant-hyperthermia and glycogen-storage-disorder sections.
